[TODAY] Eight years of braking, then Mercury caught it. ☀️

On Nov. 21, the European-Japanese BepiColombo mission slipped into orbit around Mercury, more than eight years after launch. Only one spacecraft had done that before: NASA's MESSENGER, from 2011 to 2015.

Why so long? Falling toward the Sun speeds a spacecraft up, so BepiColombo braked with nine flybys of Earth, Venus and Mercury.

Reality check: a software issue cut the final braking burn short. ESA says the spacecraft is safe while teams investigate. Its two orbiters are planned to split in December, with science from April 2027.

[TODAY] Mars rover missed 25 heartbeats in a row. 🔴

On Oct. 30, Perseverance's main radio stopped sending its regular pings to the rover's computer. After about 100 seconds of silence, the rover switched to its backup radio, which then turned out to transmit at only about half power. It now talks straight to Earth at a slower rate, so science is paused.

In orbit, NASA's Odyssey lost a reaction wheel it needs to point itself. Without a fix, its fuel can hold it steady for only one to two months.

Reality check: both are stable. NASA hopes they return to science by late November.

[TODAY] Why launch rockets from a jungle coast? 🚀

Europe's Spaceport sits at Kourou, French Guiana, on a coast at the edge of the jungle, just over 500 km north of the equator. Near the equator, Earth's spin carries the ground east at high speed. A rocket launched eastward keeps that speed for free: about 460 m/s, or roughly 1,650 km/h, according to ESA.

That means less fuel to carry and heavier satellites to lift. Rockets also fly out over open sea, where spent stages fall harmlessly.

Reality check: the boost only helps launches heading east. An Ariane 6 was scheduled to launch from Kourou on Nov. 24.

Save this for the next launch you watch.

[TODAY] Trained on cats, it confirmed a black hole. 🕳️

In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope showed the first image of a black hole: a glowing ring in the galaxy M87, about 55 million light-years away. Some asked whether the ring came partly from data processing.

A team of four at CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, built a new AI method trained only on everyday photos like cats, dogs and cars. On the original data, it found the same ring, matching a black hole of about 6.5 billion Suns. The study appeared in Nature on Nov. 12.

Reality check: it reanalyzes existing data. Fine details of the ring still differ slightly.

[IMAGINE] Past 75% light speed, some light pushes back. ✨

What is real: light carries momentum, so a powerful laser could push a thin, ultralight sail. A 2026 study from China's Harbin Institute of Technology modeled one at extreme speed. As it races away, each push gets weaker. Past about 75% of light speed, light scattered off the sail starts acting as drag, though the net push still points forward.

Reality check: it's an arXiv preprint that treats the sail as a perfect mirror and leaves out dust and heat.

The speculation: what if laser sails one day carried tiny probes to another star?
